questions.question_text: Which personality disorder is the most likely in a 23-year-old man who is sensitive to rebuffs and avoids close contact as a result?
questions.explanation:
Clinical features of patients with paranoid personality disorder include being suspicious that others are exploiting, harming, or deceiving them; reading hidden demeaning or threatening meanings into benign remarks/events; holding long-standing grudges; believing that others are not loyal or trustworthy; being reluctant to confide in others; feeling that others are attacking their character or reputation; having recurrent suspicions of infidelity.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 562.

Being vengeful, he emptied his weekly rubbish collection into their backyard before going in person to council office to make a complaint. He has always had trouble with different neighbours and has changed 9 houses in last 3 years.
questions.explanation:
Clinical features of patients with paranoid personality disorder include being suspicious that others are exploiting, harming, or deceiving them; reading hidden demeaning or threatening meanings into benign remarks/events; holding long-standing grudges; believing that others are not loyal or trustworthy; being reluctant to confide in others; feeling that others are attacking their character or reputation; having recurrent suspicions of infidelity.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 562.

questions.question_text: An 8 year old child presents with sudden movements and vocalisations, as well repetitive rituals. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Tic disorders are characterised by brief, sudden, repetitive movements (motor tics) or utterances (phonic or vocal tics) that are temporarily suppressible and are usually preceded by a strong urge to perform the tic. The most common cause of childhood-onset tics is Tourette syndrome (chronic motor tic(s) and vocal tic(s)). The most common comorbidities in Tourette syndrome include ADHD, obsessive-compulsive disorder or behaviour (OCD/B) and autism spectrum disorder. Clinical features of OCD are obsessions (intrusive, repetitive, and distressing thoughts or images) and compulsions (repetitive, stereotyped, unnecessary behaviours).
Ref: International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed. ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020) Eapen V et al. Comorbidities, social impact, and quality of life in Tourette syndrome. Frontiers in psychiatry. 2016 Jun 6;7:97.
Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 690.

questions.question_text: In ICD-11, psychotic symptoms may be present in which severity/severities of depression?
questions.explanation:
In ICD-11, depressive episodes in depressive or bipolar disorders may be described in detail by using qualifiers indicating the presence of specific symptoms: the melancholic features qualifier, the anxiety symptoms qualifier, the panic attacks qualifier, and the seasonal pattern qualifier. Additionally, depressive episodes can be described according to severity (mild, moderate, or severe) and remission status (in partial or in full remission). For moderate and severe depressive episodes, the presence of psychotic symptoms may also be indicated.
Ref: Gaebel W et al. Changes from ICD-10 to ICD-11 and future directions in psychiatric classification. Dialogues in clinical neuroscience. 2020 Mar;22(1):7.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a type of narcissistic defences?
questions.explanation:
Persons with narcissistic personality disorder have a grandiose sense of self-importance; they consider themselves special and expect special treatment. They handle criticism poorly and may become enraged when someone dares criticize them, or they may appear utterly indifferent to criticism. They are commonly interpersonally exploitative, and their self-esteem is fragile. They use primitive defence mechanisms, including projection which involves attributing one’s own internal unacceptable ideas and impulses to an external target, such as another individual, and reacting accordingly to them.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 565.
Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 892.

questions.question_text: Select one typical feature of depressive episode with psychotic symptoms

options.text: Prominent affective symptoms and mood congruent delusions
Non prominent affective symptoms and mood congruent delusions

correct_answer.text: Prominent affective symptoms and mood congruent delusions

correct_answers.text: Prominent affective symptoms and mood congruent delusions

questions.explanation:
In depression with psychotic symptoms, usually there is pervasive depressed mood (no reactivity) and marked psychomotor disturbance (sometimes to the point of depressive stupor/catatonia) accompanying delusions (commonly) and hallucinations (10-20%). Psychotic symptoms may be categorised as either mood-congruent, that is, in harmony with the mood disorder (‘I deserve punishment because I am so bad’), or mood-incongruent, not in harmony with the mood disorder. Patients with mood-incongruent psychotic symptoms are more likely to have a primary psychotic disorder, such as schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 251.
Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 380.

questions.question_text: A 27-year-old soldier returns from war field with distressing feelings, flashbacks, nightmares, and hypervigilance. Which of the following diagnosis is likely?
questions.explanation:
Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is a severe psychological disturbance following a traumatic event, characterised by involuntary re- experiencing of elements of the event, with symptoms of hyperarousal, avoidance, and emotional numbing.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 402.

questions.question_text: Clock drawing test can be used to detect
questions.explanation:
A number of cognitive, motor and perceptual functions are required simultaneously for successful completion of the clock drawing test. Clock drawing is a useful screening technique that is sensitive to organisation and planning as well as constructional ability.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 53.

questions.question_text: A 42-year-old man presents with motor clumsiness, poor coordination and unsteadiness of gait. He is apathetic and his thinking process is slowed. He has a strong family history of similar presentations. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Huntington disease (HD) is a rare neurodegenerative disorder of the central nervous system with autosomal dominant inheritance. It is characterised by chorea, dystonia, rigidity, akathisia, swallowing difficulties, myoclonus, gait and balance difficulties, bruxism, cognitive decline, psychiatric disorders, and behavioural changes (most common = lack of initiative). Diagnosis is straightforward if a patient with a known family history of HD presents with the typical neurological movement disorder (gene testing not required if there is laboratory confirmation of the Huntington’s disease gene in the family). In a patient without a family history, gene testing is essential but does not give a clinical diagnosis and must of combined with clinical history and physical exam.
Ref: Kumar A et al. Therapeutic Advances for Huntington’s Disease. Brain Sciences. 2020 Jan;10(1):43.
Bachoud-Lévi AC et al. International Guidelines for the treatment of Huntington’s Disease. Frontiers in neurology. 2019;10:710.

options.text: It is very important that you take your tablets
How many times have you missed your tablets so far?
Why are you not taking your tablets?
Is there any difficulty with your tablets?

correct_answer.text: Is there any difficulty with your tablets?

correct_answers.text: Is there any difficulty with your tablets?

questions.explanation: Asking "Is there any difficulty with your tablets?" is less judgmental and least confrontational among all the other given options.

questions.question_text: Mr Z is a 29-year-old gentleman with history of memory loss and personality changes. He also presents with wing beating tremors. The biochemical abnormality to be identified in this case would be
questions.explanation:
Wilson disease (WD) is a genetic disorder of copper metabolism that leads to copper accumulation in various organs, primarily the liver and brain. Clinical symptoms are a result of organ dysfunction due to the direct or indirect effects of copper accumulation. The underlying mechanism is the failure of copper transport in hepatocytes with subsequent impairment of incorporation into the ceruloplasmin and excretion into the bile and blood. Low ceruloplasmin may be an initial test for WD but has low sensitivity as a sole assessment. WD is typically described as a hepato-neurological disease, with focus on signs of liver disease and extrapyramidal symptoms (e.g. wing-beating tremor and dystonia).
Ref: Litwin T et al. Psychiatric manifestations in Wilson’s disease: possibilities and difficulties for treatment. Therapeutic advances in psychopharmacology. 2018 Jul;8(7):199-211.
Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 158.

questions.question_text: A patient is suspected to have parietal damage related to a vascular lesion. Which of the following signs may be elicited in neurological examination?
questions.explanation: Lower homonymous quadrantanopias are usually caused by damage to the optic radiation as it passes through the parietal lobes.

questions.question_text: An anorexic patient repeatedly purges with laxatives. Which of the following is a possible complication?
questions.explanation:
Laxative abuse in anorexia nervosa can result in metabolic acidosis. In laxative induced diarrhoea, a large amount of bicarbonate may be lost in the stool. With normal kidneys, the lost bicarbonate is replaced effectively, and a serious base deficit does not develop. When there is poor renal blood flow due to hypovolaemia/starvation, base deficit and acidosis develop rapidly. Acidosis also results from excessive production of lactic acid when patients have severe diarrhoea. Hypokalaemic/ hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis can occur from repeated vomiting.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 414.

questions.question_text: Which test would you use to screen the cognitive functioning of an elderly patient at the bedside?
questions.explanation:
The Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) is a 30-item questionnaire used for bedside cognitive testing. It is increasingly used in preference to the MMSE due to its assessment of a broader range of cognitive domains and its greater sensitivity and specificity for mild cognitive impairment. A score of below 26 suggests impairment. It is available in many languages and in electronic form.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 86.

options.text: Type I third degree heart block

questions.explanation: Mobitz type I AV block: The PR interval shows progressive lengthening until one P wave fails to be conducted and fails to produce a QRS complex. The PR interval resets to normal, and the cycle repeats. This is second-degree atrioventricular nodal block, also known as Wenckebach block.(Ref: Houghton & Gray, Making sense of the ECG. Pg 120-122)

questions.question_text: 'I saw a blue caravan on the road and I immediately realised that the South Pole is going to sink soon'. This is consistent with
questions.explanation:
A delusional perception is a primary delusion which is recalled as having arisen as a result of a perception (e.g. a patient who, on seeing two white cars pull up in front of his house, became convinced that he was therefore about to be wrongly accused of being a paedophile). The percept is a real external object, not a hallucinatory experience.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 107.

questions.question_text: Cameron described the following form of thought disorder:
questions.explanation:
Norman Cameron's analysis of formal thought disorder in 25 'unmistakably schizophrenia' patients led to the concept of asyndetic thinking that included derailment, loss of the central determining idea, and loose associations. He emphasised the lack of connections between successive thoughts in this phenomenon of ‘asyndesis’. For example, ‘I got up at eight this morning as well as few birds of different colours on the painting, shrinking all the time to drop few coins. On the floor. All the time.’ Cameron also proposed 3 other characteristic formal thought disorders –
Metonymy: imprecise approximate expressions used as substitute words. For example paperskate for a pen.
Overinclusion: In overinclusive thinking ideas that are only remotely related to the concept under consideration become incorporated in the patient's thinking; Conceptual boundaries are lost.
Interpenetration: Irrelevant thoughts penetrate ongoing stream of thoughts.
He also described thought fragmentation, similar to Schneider's derailment concept (see below)
Carl (not Kurt) Schneider proposed a different set of 5 elements of formal thought disorder.
Substitution: one thought – often inappropriate, fills the gap between other appropriate, more consistent thoughts.
Omission: A chunk of thought goes missing from stream of conversation, patient being unaware – best analysed when written.
Fusion: various thoughts fuse together, leading to loss of goal direction.
Drivelling: disordered intermixture of constituent parts of one complex thought
Derailment (aka entgleisen); In derailment normally flowing track of thoughts suddenly change. The determining tendency is preserved but is misdirected.
Schneider also described desultory thinking, sometimes considered along with driveling. In desultory thinking, speech is grammatically correct but sudden ideas force their way in from time to time. Each one of these ideas is a simple thought that, if used at the right time would be quite appropriate.
Ref: Jerónimo J et al. Formal Thought Disorders–Historical Roots. Frontiers in psychiatry. 2018 Nov 9;9:572.

questions.question_text: A patient describes that everything around him appears hazy, dull and lifeless. This can be termed as
questions.explanation:
Derealisation is an unpleasant subjective experience where the patient feels as if the world has become unreal. It is a feeling that one’s environment has changed in some strange way that is difficult to describe. Derealisation is a non-specific symptom of a number of disorders.
Depersonalisation is an unpleasant subjective experience where the patient feels as if they have become ‘unreal’. It is a feeling that one is not oneself or that something has changed. Depersonalisation is a non-specific symptom occurring in many psychiatric disorders, as well as in ‘normal’ people.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 108.
Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 10.

questions.question_text: When asked about his favorite sport the patient answers, "I like soccer. The players wear shirts. Shirts are clothes. Clothes are dirty." The speech disturbance noted here is best described as
questions.explanation:
In flight of ideas thoughts follow each other rapidly; there is no general direction of thinking; and the connections between successive thoughts appear to be due to chance factors which, however, can usually be understood. The patient’s speech is easily diverted by external stimuli and internal superficial associations. The absence of a determining tendency to thinking allows the associations of the train of thought to be determined by chance relationships, verbal associations of all kinds, clang associations, proverbs, maxims, and cliches. The chance linkage of thoughts in flight of ideas is demonstrated by the fact that one could completely reverse the sequence of the record of a flight of ideas, and the progression of thought would be understood just as well (or just as poorly).
Ref: Casey P, Kelly B. Fish’s clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4th Edition. 2019. p. 44.

questions.question_text: The nature of conversational speech in jargon dysphasia is

options.text: The rhythm of speech is not retained

questions.explanation:
Jargon aphasia is a form of fluent aphasia characterised by a copious flow of unintelligible speech. Jargon-aphasic speech may be subdivided into semantic jargon, in which ordinary words are strung together to form unintelligible utterances, and phonemic jargon involving neologisms.
Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: According to the World Health Organization, how many women have experienced intimate partner violence or non-partner sexual violence in their lifetime?
questions.explanation:
According to the World Health Organisation, almost 1 in 3 women have experienced one or both of these forms of violence (intimate partner violence or non-partner sexual violence) at least once in their lifetime. This recent data confirms that physical and sexual intimate partner violence and sexual violence more broadly remain pervasive in the lives of women and adolescent girls across the globe.
Ref: World Health Organization. Violence against women prevalence estimates, 2018: global, regional and national prevalence estimates for intimate partner violence against women and global and regional prevalence estimates for non-partner sexual violence against women. 2021.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is an example of an ideology that emphasizes the rights of groups over the individual?
questions.explanation: Group rights, also known as collective rights, are rights held by a group rather than by its individual members, the latter of which is termed individualism.

questions.question_text: William and Diane Corndale are seeking help for infertility. They have been trying to conceive for 5 years, but have so far been unsuccessful. Which of the following is the most likely consequence of this stressor?

options.text: Decrease in frequency of sexual intercourse

questions.explanation: Difficulty in conceiving may place significant stress on a couple, and there's the potential for a wide spectrum of psychological struggles to ensue.

questions.question_text: In his 1987 book, Le Suicide, what did sociologist Emile Durkheim conclude?

options.text: The risk of suicide is fixed
Suicide was more common during times of war
Suicide rates are higher in women than in men
Suicide could be attributed to a lack of social cohesion
Suicide was more common in civilians than in soldiers

correct_answer.text: Suicide could be attributed to a lack of social cohesion

correct_answers.text: Suicide could be attributed to a lack of social cohesion

questions.explanation:
Emile Durkheim was a French sociologist who challenged the assumption that social processes can be understood in terms of the actions of individuals and argued that even suicide, apparently the ultimately individualistic act, cannot be fully explained at the purely individual level. In his book Suicide, Durkheim used survey data purporting to show that egoistic suicide, resulting from feelings of self-reproach and sense of failure, arises from a lack of social cohesion; that altruistic suicide, carried out for the benefit of others, arises from a sense of failure to society; and that anomic suicide, arising from a sense that life is pointless, arises from an absence of social norms that he called anomie.
Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: Mr Loughton has come to see you in clinic, following a referral from the police. You are aware that your colleague will want to know what his future risk of sexual violence will be. Which of the following is the strongest predictive factor for future sexual violence?
questions.explanation:
History of sexual violence perpetration is the strongest predictor of sexual violence perpetration.
Ref: Steele B et al. Risk and Protective Factors for Men’s Sexual Violence Against Women at Higher Education Institutions: A Systematic and Meta-Analytic Review of the Longitudinal Evidence. Trauma, Violence, & Abuse. 2020 Nov 11:1524838020970900.

questions.question_text: Mandip is a 33-year-old Sikh male from India. He is an IT contractor and speaks English at work. He regularly goes to the pub after work for drinks with his colleagues. When he goes home he speaks Punjabi with his parents and wears traditional robes. What form of acculturation does Mandip display?
questions.explanation: Acculturation refers to the process of cultural change that takes place when an individual or a group comes in to continuous contact with a culturally distinct group. Acculturation can result from immigration and can occur in either direction – hosts can get accultured; this was evident in certain places in times of Colonial rule. Four types are described according to the degree of retention and adoption of the two cultures at ethnocultural group level. Integration refers to both high retention of one‘s own cultural values and high adoption of the practices of the new culture.

questions.question_text: Empathy skills are most likely to be delayed in which of the following?

options.text: A deaf child of deaf parents
A hearing child of deaf parents
A deaf child of hearing parents
A hearing child with one deaf parent
A hearing child of hearing parents

correct_answer.text: A deaf child of hearing parents

correct_answers.text: A deaf child of hearing parents

questions.explanation:
Many deaf children from hearing families have seriously delayed development of empathy and theory of mind (ToM). They often continue to fail false belief and other standard preschool ToM tests well into middle childhood. However, natively signing deaf children of deaf parents develop ToM understanding on the same early timetable as hearing children. This suggests the importance of shared conversation with family members via a mutually accessible language (either signed or spoken) for the development of ToM. In deaf children of hearing parents empathy and ToM are significantly correlated, unlike in hearing children where these two are less dependent.
Ref: Peterson CC. Empathy and theory of mind in deaf and hearing children. Journal of deaf studies and deaf education. 2016 Apr
1;21(2):141-7.

questions.question_text: Michael Stills is 32 years old and has developed depression for the first time in in his life. You meet him and take a history. Which of the following is a precipitating factor for his depression?

options.text: Growing up in a large city
Being married for the past 2 years
Having a parent who has a diagnosis of chronic anxiety disorder
The recent loss of his baby son from cot death at the age of 4 months

correct_answer.text: The recent loss of his baby son from cot death at the age of 4 months

correct_answers.text: The recent loss of his baby son from cot death at the age of 4 months

questions.explanation:
Four ‘Ps’ of case formulation:
Predisposing factors: those that put a person at risk of developing a problem; may include genetics, previous life events, or temperament Precipitating factors: a specific event or trigger to the onset of the current problem
Perpetuating factors: those that maintain the problem once it has become established
Protective factors: strengths that reduce the severity of problems and promote healthy and adaptive functioning
Ref: Racine NM et al. Systematic review: predisposing, precipitating, perpetuating, and present factors predicting anticipatory distress to painful medical procedures in children. Journal of pediatric psychology. 2016 Mar 1;41(2):159-81.

questions.question_text: Selina has had a spider phobia since she was a child. It impairs her ability to function, as she avoids any places whereby she might come across a spider: non-urban areas, public places that do not appear spotless. Her greatest fear is having a spider crawl over her face. She agrees to participate in some talking therapy to help her with her phobia. In one session, the therapist gives a very detailed description of a spider crawling across Selina's face. Her task is to withstand the anxiety until it diminishes in intensity. What method is this describing?
questions.explanation:
By exposing the patient to the phobic object and preventing the usual escape or avoidance, there is extinction of the usual (maladaptive) anxiety response. This may be done in vivo (flooding) or in imagination (implosion).
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 908.

questions.question_text: Two medications have the same efficacy but Drug A is marketed as having a 50% failure rate whilst Drug B is marketed as having a 50% success rate. Drug B is prescribed more frequently. What is this an example of?
questions.explanation:
The framing effect is an example of cognitive bias, in which people react to a particular choice in different ways depending on how it is presented; e.g. as a loss or as a gain. It is an effect of the description, labelling, or presentation of a problem or responses to it. In this question, the two frames are merely different ways of describing the same thing.
Heuristics are simple, efficient rules which people often use to form judgments and make decisions. The outcome bias is an error made in evaluating the quality of a decision when the outcome of that decision is already known. The Barnum effect is a common psychological phenomenon whereby individuals will give high accuracy ratings to descriptions of their personality that supposedly are tailored specifically to them but that are, in fact, vague and general enough to apply to a wide range of people. The Hawthorne effect is the alteration of behaviour by the subjects of a study due to their awareness of being observed.
Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: 'Internal salience' is a concept in psychology relating to cognitive processes. Which of the following is the most accurate description of it?

options.text: A belief that a particular object or person is important
Rating one's own thoughts as being more important than those of others
Rating one's own beliefs above factual information
Self-motivated desire for an object or action
Yearning for reminders of loved ones or objects

correct_answer.text: Self-motivated desire for an object or action

correct_answers.text: Self-motivated desire for an object or action

questions.explanation: Motivational salience is a cognitive process and a form of attention that motivates, or propels, an individual's behaviour towards or away from a particular object, perceived event, or outcome. This can be driven by external factors, such as encouragement or instruction from a teacher or similar, or internal, from within an individual due to their pre-existing beliefs.

questions.question_text: There are various factors, which influence group dynamics and impact upon their effectiveness. Which of the following factors can reduce the cohesiveness of a group?
questions.explanation:
Role ambiguity refers to the lack of clear definition of what is expected of an individual, with respect to the goals of their team. The more uncertainty there is about the tasks, goals and levels of performance, the less satisfied workers tend to be. But in the presence of task and social cohesion job satisfaction improves greatly.
Ref: Urien B, Osca A, García-Salmones L. Role ambiguity, group cohesion and job satisfaction. Revista Latinoamericana de Psicología. 2017 May 1;49(2):137-45.

questions.question_text: Attention results in the conversion of:

options.text: Short term memory into long term memory
Working memory into short term memory
Sensory memory into short term memory

correct_answer.text: Sensory memory into short term memory

correct_answers.text: Sensory memory into short term memory

questions.explanation: Sensory receptors in the brain are responsible for receiving sensory information which they store for mere seconds. The brain filters this multifaceted sensory information from multiple sensory organs. When conscious attention is paid, this certain sensory information is selected and converted into short-term memory which enables us to remember it.

questions.question_text: Working memory can be tested at bedside using which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Explanation
Digit span tests working memory by asking the participant to recall sequences of numbers of increasing lengths in a forward or backward manner. It requires patients to repeat longer strings of digits increasingly as a way of assessing the ability to process relatively simple information.
Cognitive estimation is used to test problem solving. Wisconsin card sorting test is used to test set shifting. Stroop test is used to test selective attention. Clock drawing test is used to test general cognitive ability in dementia.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 54.

questions.question_text: Anna is 8 years old. You are conducting some exercises to determine what stage of development she appears to be at, according to Piaget's stages of development. You present her with two glasses, both of the same shape, and both holding the same amount of orange juice. You then obtain two other glasses of different shapes: one is tall and thin, another short and broad. You pour the orange juice from one of the original glasses into the tall glass, and the juice from the other original glass into the shorter glass. You now ask Anna to tell you which glass holds the most juice. What answer indicates she has reached the concrete operational stage of development?

options.text: 'The short glass has the most orange juice'
'They each have more orange juice than before'
'Glasses can be half empty or half full'
'Both glasses have the same amount of orange juice'
'The tall glass has the most orange juice'

correct_answer.text: 'Both glasses have the same amount of orange juice'

correct_answers.text: 'Both glasses have the same amount of orange juice'

questions.explanation:
According to Piaget, the stage of concrete operations lasts from about 7 to 11 years of age. In this period, children operate and act on the concrete, real, and perceivable world of objects and events. Egocentric thought is replaced by operational thought, which involves dealing with a wide array of information outside the child. Children can now see things from someone else’s perspective. Children also understand the concept of conservation, which is the ability to recognise that, although the shape of objects may change, the objects still maintain or conserve other characteristics that enable them to be recognised as the same. The ability of children to understand quantity is one of Piaget’s most important cognitive developmental theories. Measures of quantity include measures of substance, length, number, liquids, and area.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. pp. 1008-1009.

questions.question_text: Which of the following of the Kohlberg's stages of moral development are paired correctly?
questions.explanation:
Lawrence Kohlberg integrated Jean Piaget’s concepts and described multiple stages of moral development within three significant levels of morality. The first level is pre-conventional morality, in which punishment and obedience are the determining factors. The second level is morality of conventional role-conformity, in which children try to conform to gain approval and maintain good relationships with others and are also guided by rigid codes of ‘law and order’ (authority orientation). The third and highest level is the morality of self-accepted moral principles (post-conventional), in which children voluntarily comply with rules based on a concept of universal ethical principles and make exceptions to rules in certain circumstances.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 902.
Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: The Oedipus complex is associated with which stage of psychosexual development?
questions.explanation:
The phallic stage begins sometime during year 3 and continues until approximately the end of year 5. Threats of castration and the related anxiety are connected with guilt over masturbation and oedipal wishes. During this phase oedipal involvement and conflict are established and consolidated.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1062.

questions.question_text: Traditionally, the view has been that boys like to play with cars and girls like to play with dolls. Which of the following is this an example of?
questions.explanation:
Socialisation is the process, beginning in infancy, whereby one acquires the attitudes, values, beliefs, habits, behaviour patterns, and accumulated knowledge of one’s society, through child-rearing, education, and modification of one’s behaviour to conform with the
demands of the society or group to which one belongs.
Indoctrination is the process of inculcating a person with ideas, attitudes, cognitive strategies or professional methodologies. A stereotype is any thought widely adopted about specific types of individuals or certain ways of behaving intended to represent the entire group of those individuals or behaviors as a whole. Normalisation refers to social processes through which ideas and actions come to be seen as "normal" and become taken-for-granted or "natural" in everyday life. Internalisation is an individual's acceptance of a set of norms and values via socialisation.
Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: Sharon lives in the same household with her younger brother who is in a same-gender partnership. Her brother and his partner want to adopt a child. Which of the following statements regarding lesbian and gay (LG), and heterosexual adoptive parents is true?

options.text: Lesbian mothers, heterosexual mothers, gay fathers, and heterosexual fathers report no differences in parenting competence in adoptive families
Heterosexual couples are more likely to adopt children than same-gender couples
Adoptive parents of all types no longer face stigma in our society
LG adoptive parents face additional stigma based on sexual identity
Stigmatisation based on sexual identity has no effect on adoptive parents' mental health

correct_answer.text: LG adoptive parents face additional stigma based on sexual identity

correct_answers.text: LG adoptive parents face additional stigma based on sexual identity

questions.explanation:
Adoptive parents of all types often face stigma related to ‘non-traditional’ family structures. Lesbian and gay (LG) adoptive parents often experience additional stigmatisation based on sexual identity, which in turn may negatively affect parents’ mental health. Children and their adoptive sexual minority parents face stigma, overt discrimination, and microaggressions based on parent sexual orientation. Lesbian mothers, heterosexual mothers, and gay fathers all report higher parenting competence than heterosexual fathers in adoptive families. Same-gender couples may be up to seven times more likely to have adoptive children than different-gendered couples.
Ref: Farr RH, Vázquez CP. Stigma Experiences, Mental Health, Perceived Parenting Competence, and Parent–Child Relationships Among Lesbian, Gay, and Heterosexual Adoptive Parents in the United States. Frontiers in psychology. 2020 Mar 30;11:445.

questions.question_text: Which of the following Erikson's stages of development are paired correctly?

options.text: 40-65 years old – ego integrity vs. despair

questions.explanation:
Erik Erikson created an original and highly influential theory of psychological development and crisis occurring in periods that extended across the entire life cycle. Stage 3 takes place from about 3 years to about 5 years. Its focus is initiative versus guilt. The child’s increasing mastery of locomotor and language skills expands its participation in the outside world and stimulates omnipotent fantasies of broader
exploration and conquest. Guilt over the drive for conquest and anxiety over the anticipated punishment are both assuaged in the child
through repression of the forbidden wishes and development of a superego to regulate its initiative.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1074.

questions.question_text: James Williams is a 2-year-old boy who is walking confidently. When he attempts to run he falls over and becomes very tearful and upset. According to Erikson‘s Psychosocial model, which of the following crises is he most likely to be experiencing?
questions.explanation:
Erik Erikson created an original and highly influential theory of psychological development and crisis occurring in periods that extended across the entire life cycle. Stage 2 takes place from about 18 months to about 3 years. Its focus is autonomy versus shame and doubt. Erikson believed that this stage “becomes decisive for the ratio between loving goodwill and hateful self-insistence, between cooperation and willfulness, and between self-expression and compulsive self-restraint or meek compliance”. Where that ratio is favourable, the child develops an appropriate sense of autonomy and the capacity to ‘have and to hold’; where it is unfavourable, doubt and shame will undermine free will.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1074.

questions.question_text: You are working with a Child and Adolescent Mental Health team, and reading about child psychosexual development. Sigmund Freud proposed a number of concepts concerning psychosexual development. Which of the following is true regarding Freud‘s theory?

options.text: The phallic stage precedes the anal stage
The Oedipus complex describes a boy‘s psychosexual competition with his mother for possession of his father
Between the ages of 6 and puberty, the child‘s libido is dormant
The genital and the phallic stages are interchangeable
In the oral phase the Oedipus complex comes into play

correct_answer.text: Between the ages of 6 and puberty, the child‘s libido is dormant

correct_answers.text: Between the ages of 6 and puberty, the child‘s libido is dormant

questions.explanation:
The latency stage is the stage of relative instinctual quiescence or inactivity of sexual drive during the period from the resolution of the Oedipus complex until pubescence (from about 5-6 years until about 11-13 years). The oral phase (age 0-1) is followed by the anal (2-3), then phallic (3-5) during which the Oedipus complex becomes activated, then latency (6-puberty), then genital (puberty).
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1063.

questions.question_text: Ms Coyle tells you that Lauren, her second eldest child, behaved in a puzzling and often upsetting way at times when she had to leave her for. She describes that Lauren would cry very dramatically at her departure, try to cling onto her, become inconsolable, would sometimes throw herself down onto the floor once she‘s left the room. The friend she left Lauren with told her that Lauren would cry for a long time and could not be comforted. When Ms Coyle returned to pick her up she‘d find Lauren to be very quiet, to look at her with a 'frozen‘ stare and wouldn‘t reach out for her for comfort. This was quite disturbing to Ms Coyle, who was expecting that Lauren would be pleased to see her, given she was so upset by the separation. What attachment style in Lauren is this vignette illustrating?
questions.explanation:
This attachment style describes often unpredictable, confusing and erratic styles of behaving towards the primary attachment figure, often born out of inconsistent or abusive care-giving.

questions.question_text: Which one among the following is the last stage of Erik Erikson's model of psychosocial development?
questions.explanation:
Erik Erikson created an original and highly influential theory of psychological development and crisis occurring in periods that extended across the entire life cycle. The last and 8th stage – integrity vs despair – takes place from about 60 years until death.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. pp. 1071-1075.

questions.question_text: Which of the following factors protects against child maltreatment in families?

options.text: History of childhood maltreatment in parents

questions.explanation:
Protective factors for child abuse and neglect include extended family networks and strong, positive social networks. Positive support from various social networks can provide a buffer to reduce caregiver stress and promote caregiver wellbeing, reducing overall maltreatment risk.
Ref: Lamont A, Price-Robertson R. Risk and protective factors for child abuse and neglect. 2013.
Austin AE et al. Risk and protective factors for child maltreatment: A review. Current epidemiology reports. 2020 Dec;7(4):334-42.

questions.question_text: According to Margaret Mahler's original theory of separation, what phase of development applies to a newborn child?
questions.explanation:
Margaret Mahler proposed a theory to describe how young children acquire a sense of identity separate from that of their mothers’. The first stage is ‘normal autism’ from birth to 2 months. In this stage, periods of sleep outweigh periods of arousal in a state reminiscent of intrauterine life.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. pp. 892-893.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is true of adolescence?

options.text: Fears of rejection for the peer group peaks around the age of 17
Negative identity is more common in societies that mark transition to adulthood by initiation ceremonies
Risk taking behaviour is less common in societies that mark transition to adulthood by initiation ceremonies
The cultural ideal hypothesis suggests that boys move further away from their physical ideal earlier than girls
Delinquency or offending behaviour reaches a peak in early teens and declines thereafter

correct_answer.text: Risk taking behaviour is less common in societies that mark transition to adulthood by initiation ceremonies

correct_answers.text: Risk taking behaviour is less common in societies that mark transition to adulthood by initiation ceremonies

questions.explanation: Initiation is a rite of passage ceremony marking entrance or acceptance into a group or society. It could also be a formal admission to adulthood in a community or one of its formal components. Risk-taking behaviour and negative identity are less common in societies that mark the transition to adulthood by initiation ceremonies. Delinquency or offending behaviour reaches a peak in late teens (17 years) and declines after that.

questions.question_text: The most common type of attachment behaviour seen in young children is
questions.explanation:
Most children are securely attached (60-70% of children). 15-20% show insecure-avoidant attachment. 10-15% show insecure-ambivalent attachment. 5-10% are disorganised in their attachment style.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 659.

questions.question_text: The game of peek-a-boo becomes characteristically evident during which stage of cognitive development in a child?
questions.explanation:
In the sensorimotor stage (birth to 2 years), infants learn to differentiate themselves from the world. They also become able to maintain a mental image of an object, even when it is not visible (object permanence). This refers to an understanding that an object that disappears from the field of perception has not ceased to exist; if searched for this object can be found, or it will reappear. It is during this stage that children play peek-a-boo.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. pp. 1007-1008.

questions.question_text: Mr Richard Parker is a 64-year-old man who has a history of paranoid schizophrenia and has been stable on the same medication regime for several years. He has recently noticed that his skin has a bluish tinge, particularly following a holiday abroad. Which of the following medications is most likely to be the cause?
questions.explanation:
Chlorpromazine is known to cause abnormal oculocutaneous pigmentation in sun-exposed areas. It can result in abnormal pigmentation of the eyelids, cornea, and lens, as well as blue-grey pigmentation of the skin.
Ref: Huff LS et al. Chlorpromazine-induced skin pigmentation with corneal and lens opacities. Cutis. 2014 May 1;93(5):247-50. Taylor DM, Gaughran F, Pillinger T. The Maudsley Practice Guidelines for Physical Health Conditions in Psychiatry. 2021. p. 519.

questions.question_text: Sandy is currently being treated for psychotic depression. She has a history of sudden cardiac death in her family and has read that some psychiatric medications can increase the risk of prolonged QTc and torsade de pointes. She has been started on an antipsychotic but is discussing with her psychiatrist which antidepressant to start. Which of the following antidepressant is most likely to cause QTC prolongation?
questions.explanation: Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. pp. 383-385.

questions.question_text: Miss Brown is a 27-year-old lady with schizoaffective disorder who has been clinically stable on risperidone for two years. She has recently reported galactorrhoea and been found to have raised prolactin. Which of the following would be the most appropriate strategy for managing her raised prolactin?
questions.explanation:
If treatment of hyperprolactinaemia is required, switching to an antipsychotic with a lower liability for prolactin elevation is usually the first choice although switching always carries a risk of destabilising the illness and relapse. An alternative is to add aripiprazole to existing treatment. Aripiprazole lowers prolactin levels in a dose-dependent manner: 3mg/day is effective but 6mg/day more so. Higher doses
appear unnecessary. Other strategies to reduce long-term risk to bone mineral density should also be discussed (e.g. stopping smoking, increasing weight-bearing exercise, and ensuring adequate calcium and vitamin D3 intake).
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 169.

questions.question_text: John is a 25-year-old man with treatment resistant schizophrenia. He is due to start an inpatient clozapine titration. He wants to know the rationale for regular blood tests and whether he is at higher risk of problems with his white blood cells. Which of the following is a risk factor for agranulocytosis in patients taking clozapine?

options.text: More than 1 year of clozapine treatment

questions.explanation:
Risk factors for agranulocytosis are different from those for neutropenia.
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 236.
Mijovic A, MacCabe JH. Clozapine-induced agranulocytosis. Annals of Hematology. 2020 Aug 20:1-6.
Silva E et al. Clozapine rechallenge and initiation despite neutropenia-a practical, step-by-step guide. BMC psychiatry. 2020 Dec;20:1-9.

questions.question_text: QT prolongation is a significant side effect of numerous medications as it can lead to torsades de pointes, a fatal arrhythmia. Which of the following medications is associated with QT prolongation?
questions.explanation:
Numerous independent risk factors for QTc interval prolongation and TdP have been identified, and include female sex, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, acute myocardial infarction, sepsis, supratherapeutic concentrations of QTc interval-prolonging drugs, rapid intravenous infusion of QTc interval-prolonging drugs, concomitant administration of two or more QTc interval-prolonging drugs, concomitant
administration of a loop diuretic, bradycardia, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, and ion channel polymorphisms. Ref: Tisdale JE. What causes some patients with drug-induced QT interval prolongation to develop torsades de pointes but not others? The elusive missing link. Drugs & aging. 2014 Aug 1;31(8):577-9.

questions.question_text: Mr. James is a 69-year-old man with Parkinson's disease on Pramipexole who has recently presented with impulse control problems including pathological gambling and some compulsive buying. His neurologist reduces his pramipexole but very quickly he appears to develop dopamine agonist withdrawal syndrome (DAWS). Which of the following symptoms are not usually seen in DAWS?
questions.explanation:
Reduction and discontinuation of dopamine agonists such as pramipexole may lead to deterioration in motor and non-motor performance. Symptoms of restless leg syndrome may be exacerbated or unmasked for the first time, as can akathisia as well as dopamine responsive non-motor symptoms such as depression, pain, apathy, and sleep disorders. Dopamine agonist withdrawal syndrome (DAWS) may occur in 15-24% of patients exhibiting neuropsychiatric symptoms (anxiety, dysphoria, panic attacks, depression, irritability, and fatigue) and autonomic symptoms (orthostatic hypotension and perspiration).
Ref: Koschel J et al. Implications of dopaminergic medication withdrawal in Parkinson’s disease. Journal of Neural Transmission. 2021 Jul 29:1-0.
