questions.question_text: Ben Staines is a 42-year-old man with a diagnosis of schizophrenia, who has been stable on Clozapine for the past year. He presents to clinic reporting low mood for the past three weeks, with loss of energy, reduced interest in life. You consider starting him on an antidepressant. Which is best to avoid, given that he is on Clozapine?
questions.explanation:
Fluoxetine is a potent inhibitor of CYP2D6 and can raise clozapine levels, resulting in increased seizure risk with clozapine.
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. pp. 308-309. Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Prescriber’s Guide, 7th Edition. 2021.

questions.question_text: In relation to weight gain with antipsychotics, which of the following statements is true:

options.text: It is more significant in children
Occurs more with first generation antipsychotics
Occurs less with second generation antipsychotics
It is more significant in adults

correct_answer.text: It is more significant in children

correct_answers.text: It is more significant in children

questions.explanation:
An increased susceptibility to antipsychotic-induced weight gain has been repeatedly documented in children, particularly rapid weight gain. Furthermore, antipsychotic medications touted to be weight-neutral in adults can cause substantial weight gain in children.
Ref: Libowitz MR, Nurmi EL. The burden of antipsychotic-induced weight gain and metabolic syndrome in children. Frontiers in Psychiatry. 2021 Mar 12;12:275.

questions.question_text: Duloxetine is an antidepressant used in the UK. Which of the following is true about it?

options.text: Doses of 120mg are routinely used for neuropathic pain
Patients with gastric bypass surgery may need a lower dose
It is a dual action antidepressant
Smoking has no impact on the plasma levels and efficacy
It has a half-life of around 36 hours

correct_answer.text: It is a dual action antidepressant

correct_answers.text: It is a dual action antidepressant

questions.explanation:
Duloxetine, along with venlafaxine, is sometimes termed as a dual action antidepressant (acts on both serotonin and noradrenaline). The elimination half-life of duloxetine is approximately 12 hours.
Usual dosage ranges are 40-60mg/day in 1-2 doses for depression, 60mg once daily for diabetic peripheral neuropathy and fibromyalgia, and 40mg twice daily for stress urinary incontinence.
Studies have not demonstrated increased efficacy of duloxetine beyond 60mg/day. Some patients may require up to or more than 120mg/day, but clinical experience is quite limited with high dosing. In neuropathic pain and fibromyalgia, doses above 60mg/day have been associated with increased side effects without an increase in efficacy.
Plasma levels of duloxetine can be reduced by up to 50% in smokers (Pg 857, Maudsley 14th) and 42% lower after gastric bypass surgery (Pg 823, Maudsley 14th). Higher dose may be necessary for these patients to achieve therapeutic benefits.
Ref: Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Prescriber’s Guide, 7th Edition. 2021. pp. 265-266.
Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. pp. 823, 857.

questions.question_text: Laura is prescribed a new antidepressant, vortioxetine. Which receptor does vortioxetine exert its action on?
questions.explanation:
Vortioxetine causes serotonin transporter (SERT) inhibition as well as having antagonist actions at 5HT3 and 5HT7 receptors, with agonist actions at 5HT1A receptors and weak partial agonist to antagonist actions at 5HT1B/D receptors. This unique blend of pharmacological actions leads to downstream release of many different neurotransmitters, and these actions hypothetically lead to antidepressant effects in unipolar depression, characterised by robust pro-cognitive actions, especially improving processing speed.
Ref: Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Neuroscientific Basis and Practical Applications, 5th Edition. 2021. p. 315.

questions.question_text: Which one among the following is a pharmacodynamic concept?
questions.explanation:
Pharmacokinetics is the study of how the body acts upon drugs, especially to absorb, distribute, metabolise, and excrete them. Pharmacodynamic actions at specific drug targets are known as the mechanism of action of psychotropic drugs, and account for most of the therapeutic effects and side effects of drugs. Agonism, receptor half-life, occupancy, dose-response relationship are pharmacodynamic concepts.
Ref: Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Neuroscientific Basis and Practical Applications, 5th Edition. 2021. p. 49.

questions.question_text: Sasha has returned home from a night out, during which she drank 12 units of alcohol. Her housemate is very worried about her, as she appears barely conscious, and decides to take her to the Emergency Department. You are aware that alcohol is eliminated in a constant amount per unit time, and that this constant does not vary according to plasma concentration of alcohol. What type of elimination kinetics is this describing?
questions.explanation: In zero order kinetics (also known as non linear kinetics) the elimination rate saturates at high drug concentrations, as occurs with alcohol, phenytoin, and salicylates, among others.

questions.question_text: The effectiveness of certain psychotropic medications can be affected by pharmacokinetics. Which of the following is an aspect of pharmacokinetics?
questions.explanation:
Pharmacokinetics is the study of how the body acts upon drugs, especially to absorb, distribute, metabolise, and excrete them. Agonism, half-life, dose-response relationship and chelation are pharmacodynamic concepts.
Ref: Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Neuroscientific Basis and Practical Applications, 5th Edition. 2021. p. 49.

questions.question_text: Psychotropic medications will sometimes enter adipose tissue and become concentrated there. What properties of a drug aid its movement into fat tissue?
questions.explanation: Lipophilic compounds enter adipose tissue more easily. The other states described would make crossing a cell membrane more difficult.

questions.question_text: Pharmacokinetics in the elderly is different to those of younger individual due to the physiological changes associated with aging. Which of the following is true regarding the volume of distribution in elderly individuals?

options.text: Lower for lipophilic and hydrophilic medications
Greater for lipophilic and hydrophilic medications

questions.explanation:
Older adults have more body fat, less body water, and less albumin than younger adults. This leads to an increased volume of distribution and a longer duration of action for some fat-soluble drugs (e.g. diazepam), higher concentrations of drugs at the site of action (e.g. digoxin), and a reduction in the amount of drug bound to albumin (increased amounts of active ‘free drug’; e.g. warfarin, phenytoin). There tends to be a greater volume of distribution for lipophilic drugs and lower for hydrophilic medications.
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 602.

questions.question_text: Pregnancy is a time of significant physiological change and this can have a significant impact upon the effect of medications. Which of the following is true regarding medication metabolism in pregnancy?
questions.explanation: The volume of distribution for hydrophilic and lipophilic drugs is increased in pregnancy due to an increase in adipose tissue, blood volume and extracellular fluid.

questions.question_text: Mrs. Jackson is an 89-year-old lady who has been taking temazepam for many years. Which of the following is correct regarding pharmacokinetics in older people?

options.text: Increase in the amount of drug bound to albumin
Dosage reduction is usually not required
Drugs excreted by the kidney rarely accumulate
Drugs are absorbed from the gut more quickly
Longer duration of action for fat soluble drugs

correct_answer.text: Longer duration of action for fat soluble drugs

correct_answers.text: Longer duration of action for fat soluble drugs

questions.explanation:
Older adults have more body fat, less body water, and less albumin than younger adults. This leads to an increased volume of distribution and a longer duration of action for some fat-soluble drugs (e.g. diazepam), higher concentrations of drugs at the site of action (e.g. digoxin), and a reduction in the amount of drug bound to albumin (increased amounts of active ‘free drug’; e.g. warfarin, phenytoin).
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 602.
Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 558.

questions.question_text: Mr. Jones visits his GP regarding his insomnia after a recent long-haul flight. His GP speaks with him and does not find any evidence of depression or other sleep disturbance. Mr. Jones is keen to try melatonin. Which one of the following statements is correct regarding the endogenous hormone melatonin?

options.text: It acts on the mu receptor
Melatonin levels are reduced in darkness
It is produced by the pituitary
It is involved in termination of sleep

questions.explanation:
The pineal gland of the epithalamus releases melatonin, perhaps the best-known circadian modulator. Release of melatonin is dependent on environmental inputs, most notably the light cycle; melatonin increases several hours after the onset of the dark phase of the light cycle, and it remains high until the restoration of the light phase the next day (levels peak between 11pm and 3am). In humans, melatonin’s effects are the principal mediator for normal sleep onset several hours into the dark phase of the diurnal cycle. There are three types of receptors for melatonin: 1 and 2 (MT1 and MT2), which are both involved in sleep, and 3, which is actually the enzyme NRH-quinine oxidoreductase 2 and not thought to be involved in sleep physiology.
Ref: Smith PC, Mong JA. Neuroendocrine control of sleep. Neuroendocrine Regulation of Behavior. 2019:353-78.
Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Neuroscientific Basis and Practical Applications, 5th Edition. 2021. p. 439.

questions.question_text: Depot antipsychotics are useful in patients who are often non-concordant with medications or who are unwilling to take tablets. Which of the following depot medications has the longest half-life?
questions.explanation:
Paliperidone is the major active metabolite of risperidone. Paliperidone palmitate is the ester prodrug of paliperidone available as a monthly and a 3-monthly long-acting injection. Kinetics for paliperidone palmitate are determined by particle size: smaller particles (1-month injectable) versus larger particles (3-month injectable). Half-life for the one-month injectable is 25-49 days. Half-life for the 3-month injectable is 84-95 days (deltoid administration) or 118-139 days (gluteal administration).
Ref: Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Prescriber’s Guide, 7th Edition. 2021. pp. 587-588.
Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. pp. 69, 72, 83.

questions.question_text: Tricyclic antidepressants are recognised as being potentially hazardous in overdose, particularly when compared to newer antidepressant medications. Which of the following is true regarding tricyclics in overdose?

options.text: They are subject to zero order kinetics
They do not bind to serum proteins

correct_answer.text: They are subject to zero order kinetics

correct_answers.text: They are subject to zero order kinetics

questions.explanation: Tricyclic antidepressants taken in large quantities altered pharmacokinetics. Their absorption may be delayed by inhibition of gastric emptying and peristalsis. A significant enterohepatic recirculation delays final elimination of a large fraction of the drug. The enzymes responsible for TCA benzyl-hydroxylation can become saturated and thus reduce TCA elimination to zero-order kinetics. They are highly protein-bound although there are more free compounds in overdose. Overdose is associated with acidosis, further delaying clearance, and tachycardia is the most common arrhythmia seen. Ref: Jarvis MR. Clinical pharmacokinetics of tricyclic antidepressant overdose. Psychopharmacology bulletin. 1991;27(4):541-50.

questions.question_text: John Wilson is a 37-year-old Caucasian male with treatment-resistant schizophrenia. He meets with his psychiatrist to discuss the potential side effects of the antipsychotic clozapine. What is the risk of agranulocytosis in a patient taking clozapine after one year?
questions.explanation:
The prevalence of agranulocytosis during clozapine treatment is 0.4%, lower than previously thought. Clozapine-induced agranulocytosis typically occurs within the first 18 weeks of treatment, with few cases occurring beyond 6 months. After 1 year of treatment, residual risk is estimated at 0.39/1000 patient/years (risk of <0.01% after one year).
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 236.
Mijovic A, MacCabe JH. Clozapine-induced agranulocytosis. Annals of Hematology. 2020 Aug 20:1-6.

questions.question_text: Mr. Davies is a 32-year-old man with a diagnosis of bipolar affective disorder who has required prolonged admissions in the past for episodes of mania. He has now presented to clinic with a severe depressive episode despite being compliant with mood stabilising medication. He is wondering about taking an antidepressant but is worried about the risk of a manic episode and refuses to take olanzapine in combination due to severe weight gain in the past. Which of the following antidepressants is least likely to induce a manic switch while already taking long-term treatment for bipolar disorder?
questions.explanation:
As reflected in the most recent bipolar guidelines, there are several options, including the addition of olanzapine+fluoxetine, quetiapine, olanzapine, or lamotrigine. But this patient refuses olanzapine.
The meta-analytical literature (Gijsman et al, 2004) provides a rate of switching for tricyclic antidepressants as 10% compared with 3.2% for all other antidepressants combined. MAOIs are also categorised to have a higher switch rate (Yatham, Kusumakar & Kutcher, 2002; Page 24). There is a 4-fold higher switch rate for venlafaxine (29%) compared with SSRIs (sertraline 9%) and bupropion (10%) when used concurrently with a mood stabilizer. Fluvoxamine may have much lower risk and newer agents such as vortioxetine may have a higher switch rate, but further studies are needed to reduce the uncertainty.
Ref: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4321017/ .
Also see Jo YT et al. Diagnostic conversion from unipolar to bipolar affective disorder: a population-based study. Journal of Affective Disorders. 2022 Jan 20.
National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence. The NICE guideline on the assessment and management of bipolar disorder in adults, children and young people in primary and secondary care. Updated edition 2020.

questions.question_text:
Sadira is a 36-year-old female from South India. She is an inpatient on your ward and was diagnosed with treatment-refractory
schizophrenia five months ago. Since then she has been treated with psychotropic medication, which she initially tolerated well. She says that her auditory hallucinations have lessened in their intensity. Previously a heavy smoker, Sadira managed to give this up recently. During the ward round she complains of feeling increasingly drowsy. You look at her medications to see if she is taking anything that may be contributing to this. Which of the following medications are most likely contributing to her current presentation?
questions.explanation:
Tobacco smoke contains polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons that induce (increase the activity of) certain hepatic enzymes (CYP1A2 in particular). The extent of enzyme induction is determined by the number and type of cigarettes smoked and the degree of smoke inhalation. For some drugs used in psychiatry, smoking significantly reduces drug plasma levels and higher doses are required than in non-smokers. Smoking reduces plasma clozapine levels by up to 50%. When people stop smoking, enzyme activity halves roughly every 2 days. Plasma levels of affected drugs will then rise, sometimes substantially. Dose reduction will usually be necessary.
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 856.

questions.question_text: Mr. Collins is a 48-year-old man with a diagnosis of alcohol dependence. He previously had 10 years of abstinence after treatment with disulfiram but relapsed 3 years ago. He is keen to have disulfiram again. Which of the following is a side-effect of disulfiram in the absence of alcohol consumption?
questions.explanation:
In the absence of alcohol consumption, side effects of disulfiram include halitosis, metallic taste, headache, dermatitis, and sedation.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 598.
Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Prescriber’s Guide, 7th Edition. 2021. p. 239.

questions.question_text: Mr Edwards is a 60-year-old man who has erectile dysfunction. He attends his GP asking about sildenafil. Which of the following is a common side-effect of this medication?
questions.explanation:
Common side effects of phosphodiesterase inhibitors (such as sildenafil and tadalafil) are mild headaches, dizziness, and nasal congestion.
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 176.

questions.question_text: A hypertensive patient develops a small focal lesion of one inferior olivary nucleus. Which of the following clinical signs can be expected?
questions.explanation: Inferior Olivary Nucleus has a role in motor coordination by providing CLIMBING FIBERS to the cerebellum.Lesion results in motor incoordination of the contralateral arm and leg (unlike other cerebellar lesions which cause ipsilateral dysfunction)

questions.question_text: A 50-year-old man on a neurology ward has non-dominant parietal lobe dysfunction. Identify the test that he is least likely to be able to do?
questions.explanation: The cognitive process tested by asking the patient to copy intersecting pentagons is constructional praxis, which is a feature of non- dominant parietal lobe lesions. The effects of lesion involving non-dominant parietal lobe include visuospatial dysfunction, topographical memory loss, and constructional / dressing apraxia. These disorders could be seen in lesions of either hemisphere but observed more frequently and are of greater severity with lesions of the non-dominant parietal lobe.

questions.question_text: Mr. Smith was seen by a clinical psychologist at a memory clinic and was noted to have features of executive dysfunction. Executive function is tested using which of the following tests?
questions.explanation:
The Wisconsin card sorting task is a test of executive functioning. It is a measure of problem-solving efficiency that is particularly sensitive to executive deficits of perseveration and impaired ability to flexibly generate alternative strategies in response to feedback. The patient has to determine the rule for card allocation and allocate cards accordingly. When the rule changes, a patient with frontal lobe dysfunction is likely to make more errors (tests response inhibition and set shifting).
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 53.
Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 88.

questions.question_text: Non-fluent expressive dysphasia is seen in which of the following conditions
questions.explanation:
Broca aphasia is also called non-fluent expressive dysphasia. There is reduced frequency and fluency of speech and presents with few disjointed words. Comprehension is relatively preserved. In frontotemporal dementia, particularly the progressive non-fluent aphasia subtype, atrophy in Broca area causes non-fluent effortful speech with agrammatism.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 160.

questions.question_text: Digit span test is administered to patient with suspected cognitive impairment. This test detects problem in which of the following cognitive faculties?
questions.explanation:
Digit span is a test of working memory (immediate) and attention. Immediate (or working) memory refers to the amount of information that can be held in mind (like a phone number or digit span) to be available for immediate use. Digit span requires patients to repeat longer strings of digits increasingly as a way of assessing the ability to process relatively simple information.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 54.

questions.question_text: The risk of schizophrenia in a monozygotic twin of schizophrenia patient compared to the general population is
questions.explanation:
Genetic factors account for most of the liability to schizophrenia. Heritability estimates range from 60-80%. The risk of developing schizophrenia if one is no relatives affected is 0.5-1%. The risk of developing schizophrenia when one has an affected identical twin is approximately 46%, about 50 times higher than the general population.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. pp. 190-191.

questions.question_text: You are seeing a patient in a gender identity clinic. The patient would like to obtain membership of a gender that they experience, which is different from the assigned gender based on sex at birth. They are also keen to be treated as a member of the experienced gender. The most probable description when using ICD-11 nomenclature is
questions.explanation:
ICD-11 Gender Incongruence, in contrast to DSM-5 Gender Dysphoria, is explicitly not a mental disorder as it requires neither distress nor dysfunction as a feature. Notably, Gender Incongruence in Childhood and in Adolescence and Adulthood does not have the label “disorder”
anymore, and are moved out of the chapter on Mental, Behavioral or Neurodevelopmental Disorders to a new ICD-11 chapter on Conditions
Related to Sexual Health. Further, unlike DSM Gender Dysphoria, a 6-months duration is not required; instead 'several months' is described as a feature.
Despite these differences, the commonalities between ICD-11 and DSM-5 are: (1) a strong dislike or discomfort with the one's sex
characteristics, (2) a strong desire to be rid of some of all of one's sex characteristics, (3) a strong desire to have the sex characteristics of the experienced gender, and (4) a strong desire to be treated (to live and be accepted) as a person of the experienced gender.
Ref: Reed, G.M., et al, 2016. Disorders related to sexuality and gender identity in the ICD‐11: revising the ICD‐10 classification based on current scientific evidence, best clinical practices, and human rights considerations. World Psychiatry, 15(3), pp.205-221.
Robles, R., et al, 2022. Validity of Categories Related to Gender Identity in ICD-11 and DSM-5 Among Transgender Individuals who Seek
Gender-Affirming Medical Procedures. International Journal of Clinical and Health Psychology, 22(1), p.100281.

questions.question_text: The presence of a single apolipoprotein-e4 allele increases the chance of developing Alzheimer's disease by around
questions.explanation:
A polymorphism in the Apolipoprotein ε4 (Chromosome 19) is a major risk factor for late- onset Alzheimer disease. Specifically, the presence of ε4 alleles increases risk of late-onset AD; people with one copy of the gene (ε3/4 heterozygotes) have 3x the incidence of Alzheimer’s disease than no ε4 gene, and people with two ε4 genes have the disease 8 times more frequently than do those with no ε4 gene (some quote a higher risk); genetic testing for presence of ε4 is not currently recommended as it is also present in people without dementia, and not found in all cases of dementia. This gene promotes the deposition of beta-amyloid protein in the brain, contributing to the formation of senile plaques.
In most populations, the ε3 allele is the most common. However, in familial late-onset Alzheimer disease, the incidence of ε4 is approximately 50%, compared with 16% in normal controls. The ancestral allele ε2, in contrast, is underrepresented.
Epidemiological studies suggest that 30-60% of late-onset Alzheimer disease cases have at least one ε4 allele. The ε4 genotype appears to be a more important risk factor for Alzheimer disease in populations of European and Asian origin when compared with populations of African origin.
Ref: Fernandez CG, Hamby ME, McReynolds ML, Ray WJ. The role of APOE4 in disrupting the homeostatic functions of astrocytes and
microglia in aging and Alzheimer’s disease. Frontiers in aging neuroscience. 2019 Feb 11;11:14.

questions.question_text: Culturing cells in conditions of thymidine deprivation has aided in the understanding of which of the following disorders?
questions.explanation:
Fragile X syndrome is associated with a rare fragile and unsteady site on Xq27. This site, named FRAXA, was originally observed as a non- staining gap, break, or constriction in the metaphase chromosomes placed under selective cultural conditions, such as folic acid or thymidine deprivation.
Ciaccio C et al. Fragile X syndrome: a review of clinical and molecular diagnoses. Italian journal of pediatrics. 2017 Dec;43(1):1-12.

questions.question_text: Social anxiety and gaze avoidance are features of which of the following trinucleotide expansion syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Fragile X syndrome is associated with a trinucleotide (CGG) triplet repeat on the distal part of the long arm of the X chromosome (Xq27.3- FMR1) that leads to the characteristic ‘fragile’ appearance of the chromosome. FMR1 gene is required for normal neural development; penetrance is low, but greater in males than females (due to the protective effects of the second normal X chromosome in females). Behavioural features are similar to those seen in ADHD and autism and include hand flapping/waving, repetitive mannerisms, shyness, gaze avoidance, poor peer relationships, communication difficulties (e.g. delayed language development, conversational rigidity, perseveration, echolalia, palilalia(repetition of syllables, words, phrases), cluttering, and over-detailed speech), and psychiatric problems (e.g. prominent depression/anxiety).
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 814.

questions.question_text: One of the following disorders do not involve genetic deletion. Choose the correct answer.
questions.explanation:
Friedreich ataxia is an autosomal recessive spinocerebellar ataxia. It is the most common inherited ataxia in Europe. In the majority of cases the disease is caused by a homozygous GAA triplet repeat expansion in the frataxin (FXN) gene, and the shorter repeat expansion length correlates with age at onset and disease severity.
Ref: Cook A, Giunti P. Friedreich’s ataxia: clinical features, pathogenesis and management. British medical bulletin. 2017 Dec 1:19-30.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is a primary proponent of endophenotypes concept?
questions.explanation:
Having broken new ground in the field of polygenicity and epigenetics, Irving Gottesman understood that unraveling the complex genomic basis of the fuzzy and qualitative diagnosis of schizophrenia would be a daunting task. How to make the task simpler, more parsimonious, and more neurobiologically meaningful? To do this, Gottesman introduced the concept of endophenotypes into the schizophrenia literature. Endophenotypes are laboratory-based measures that show deficits in schizophrenia patients and lesser deficits in their first-degree ‘unaffected’ relatives and are viewed as being more proximal to genes and having a simpler genetic architecture than are ‘fuzzy’ qualitative diagnostic disorders.
Ref: Braff DL, Tamminga CA. Endophenotypes, epigenetics, polygenicity and more: Irv Gottesman’s dynamic legacy. Schizophrenia bulletin. 2017 Jan 1;43(1):10-6.

questions.question_text: The process of meiosis produces
questions.explanation:
Meiosis is a form of cell division in which the nucleus divides into four daughter nuclei, each containing half the chromosomes of the parent nucleus. It consists of two consecutive divisions: during the first, homologous chromosomes pair up, exchange genetic material by crossing over (‘recombination’), then during the anaphase part of the cycle move apart by disjunction to form separate haploid nuclei. During the second phase, these daughter nuclei divide by mitosis (with a further anaphase), producing four haploid cells.
Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is best termed as an intermediate phenotype with high occurrence in relatives but cannot be justifiably classified as an endophenotype for schizophrenia?
questions.explanation:
Predominantly, neurological soft signs (NSS) have been looked at as endophenotypes (i.e., hardcopies of the genetic liability) and thus a trait phenomenon. However, the literature on NSS in schizophrenia presents at least partially diverging results. On the one hand, research speaks in favour of NSS as being a stable entity (i.e., a trait): NSS are more pronounced in patients compared to their relatives; they are present at disease onset; there is a relationship with the most stable symptoms, namely negative and cognitive ones. On the other hand, there are arguments supporting a fluctuating aspect, especially of motor signs. Only the presence of a trait can be used as an
endophenotype or a predictor, but not the quantitative expression (i.e., the state). Thus, the usage of NSS as an endophenotype has to be called into question.
The most established endophenotypes for schizophrenia are changes in neurocognition (attention deficits, working and verbal declarative memory dysfunctions) and neurophysiology (pre-pulse inhibition, anti-saccade impairment, event-related potential deficits) (Donati et al., 2020).
Ref: Bachmann S, Schröder J. Neurological soft signs in schizophrenia: an update on the state-versus trait-perspective. Frontiers in psychiatry. 2018 Jan 8;8:272.
Donati FL, D’Agostino A, Ferrarelli F. Neurocognitive and neurophysiological endophenotypes in schizophrenia: An overview. Biomarkers in Neuropsychiatry. 2020 Dec 1;3:100017.

questions.question_text: The Kluver-Bucy syndrome is typically associated with lesions of which of the following structures?
questions.explanation:
In 1937, Heinrich Kluver and Paul Bucy described a dramatic behavioural syndrome in monkeys after bilateral temporal lobectomy. The full Kluver-Bucy syndrome (KBS) – hyperorality, placidity, hypermetamorphosis, dietary changes, altered sexual behaviour, and visual agnosia – is evident within 3 weeks following operation. By the 1970s, it was clear that the major symptoms of KBS are produced by destroying either the temporal neocortex or the amygdala bilaterally. The clinical features of KBS in humans are similar to those in monkeys, but the full syndrome is rarely seen, probably because the anterior temporal lobe dysfunction is usually less severe than that following total temporal lobe ablation in monkeys.
Ref: Lanska DJ. The Klüver-Bucy syndrome. Neurologic-Psychiatric Syndromes in Focus-Part I. 2018;41:77-89.

questions.question_text: The last part of the brain to mature is
questions.explanation:
The last area of the brain to develop is the frontal lobe. The last region of the brain to mature is pre-frontal cortex (anterior frontal pole). While it may be fully formed in size, various parts within the structure of the brain continue to develop well into a person's twenties. The adolescent brain is immature and in a dynamic state of development. Frontal brain development is also a factor related to impulsive
behavior among teens.

questions.question_text: Hypothetical use of cholecystokinin has been studied in which of the following disorders?
questions.explanation:
Neurobiological disturbances are present in individuals with bulimia nervosa and may increase the probability of binge eating. In particular, individuals with the disorder tend to display delayed gastric emptying, increased stomach capacity, and reduced secretion of
cholecystokinin, a peptide hormone released by the small intestine that helps to signal satiety during food consumption.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 479.

questions.question_text: The enzyme involved in degradation of noradrenaline in presynaptic neurons is
questions.explanation:
Norepinephrine (NE) action is terminated by two principal destructive or catabolic enzymes that turn NE into inactive metabolites. The first is monoamine oxidase A or B, which is located in mitochondria in the presynaptic neuron and elsewhere. The second is catechol-O-
methyltransferase (COMT), which is thought to be located largely outside of the presynaptic nerve terminal. The action of NE can be terminated not only by enzymes that destroy NE, but also by a transport pump for NE that removes it from acting in the synapse without destroying it. That transport pump is sometimes called the ‘NE transporter’ or ‘NET’ and sometimes the ‘NE reuptake pump’.
Ref: Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Neuroscientific Basis and Practical Applications, 5th Edition. 2021. pp. 253-254.

questions.question_text: Which of the following receptors requires the simultaneous binding of two different agonists for activation?
questions.explanation:
Glutamate systems are curious in that one of the key receptors for glutamate (the NMDA receptor) requires a co-transmitter in addition to glutamate in order to function. The co-transmitter is either the amino acid glycine or another amino acid, closely related to glycine, known as D-serine.
Ref: Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Neuroscientific Basis and Practical Applications, 5th Edition. 2021. pp. 97-98.

questions.question_text: Which of the following pathological bodies is made up of ubiquitin and alpha synuclein and is associated with loss of dopaminergic neurons in basal ganglia?
questions.explanation:
The key constituent of Lewy bodies is alpha-synuclein. When aggregates of misfolded, overexpressed alpha-synuclein accumulate in neurons or surrounding glial cells, Lewy bodies are formed. Lewy bodies are immunoreactive for alpha-synuclein as well as for ubiquitin and alpha- beta-crystallin. Neuropathic changes of dementia with Lewy bodies include the presence of Lewy bodies and Lewy neurites in the cerebral cortex as well as in the brainstem. These are often accompanied by some degree of Alzheimer disease neuropathologic changes, often with a moderate beta-amyloid plaque burden but relatively lower tangle burden.
Ref: Sanford AM. Lewy body dementia. Clinics in geriatric medicine. 2018 Nov 1;34(4):603-15.
Gray F, Duyckaerts C, de Girolami U. Escourolle and Poirier’s Manual of Basic Neuropathology, 6th Edition. 2019. pp. 6-7, 197.

questions.question_text: A 55 year old lady presents with weakness of her legs and hands. She feels clumsy with a history of falls. On examination she has fasciculations in her tongue and memory deficits. She is diagnosed to have amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. The primary pathological change will be noted in
questions.explanation:
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is characterised by degeneration of both upper motor neurons (UMNs) and lower motor neurons (LMNs). While the balance between the severity and pace of involvement of these two sets of neurons may vary from case to case, the combination is characteristic of ALS. In many cases, the disease begins with involvement of spinal LMNs, manifesting as weakness in the arms or legs. In others, ALS begins with bulbar symptoms and may be termed progressive bulbar palsy.
Ref: Gray F, Duyckaerts C, de Girolami U. Escourolle and Poirier’s Manual of Basic Neuropathology, 6th Edition. 2019. p. 215.

questions.question_text: Which of the following accounts for spongiform appearance in CJD?
questions.explanation:
Neuropathologic findings in Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) are characterised by spongiform changes secondary to neuropil vacuolation. Vacuolated neurons and/or vacuolated neuropil is observed typically in CJD.
Ref: Iwasaki Y. Creutzfeldt‐Jakob disease. Neuropathology. 2017 Apr;37(2):174-88.
Gray F, Duyckaerts C, de Girolami U. Escourolle and Poirier’s Manual of Basic Neuropathology, 6th Edition. 2019. p. 4.
